StringWithMarkup.String: Octachlorostyrene (CAS # 29082-74-4) was evaluated for chronic toxicity in weanling Sprague-Dawley rats (20/sex/group) exposed to concentrations of 0 (corn oil vehicle control), 0.005, 0.05, 0.5, 5.0, or 50 ppm in ad libitum diet for 12 months. The actual doses ranged from 0.0003-3.1 mg/kg bodyweight/day and 0.0004-4.4 mg/kg/day, respectively, for males and females. Mortality in 7 males and 2 females between 6 months and 1 year did not appear related to treatment and no clinical toxicity was observed. Bodyweights of 0.005, 0.5, and 50 ppm males increased, while food consumption was comparable to that of controls. In both males and females, 50 ppm exposures induced significantly (Duncan's multiple range test, p < 0.05) increased hepatosplenomegaly (relative liver to bodyweight). Aniline hydroxylase and aminopyrine demethylase activity were elevated in hepatic microsomes of 5.0 ppm males and 50.0 ppm males and females. Residues of octachlorostyrene (mean per g wet tissues from 5 or more rats) in liver and fat tissues of males and females increased in conjunction with level of dietary exposure from 0.5 ppm. Although the relationship to exposure level was not linear, the authors acknowledged the lipophilic nature of octachlorostyrene and anticipated accumulation in adipose tissue. The organ targets of octachlorostyrene toxicity were identified as the liver, thyroid, and kidney, the changes in the thyroid showed dose-related severity and frequency at high dose levels. Microscopic treatment-related liver changes included increased morphological zonation, nuclear anisokaryosis, cytoplasmic vacuolation, and moderate to severe hepatocellular eosinophilia and basophilia. In the thyroid, treatment induced reduced colloid density, focal collapse of follicles, and epithelial thickening with moderate to severe focal vacuolation and papillary proliferation. At doses up to 0.5 ppm, the kidney exhibited multiple adhesions in glomeruli and thickening of basement membrane, while at doses above 5.0 ppm and above the kidney showed significant dose-related dilation of proximal tubules and cytoplasmic eosinophilia along with granular casts and proteinaceous losses. Tumor incidence was infrequent and appeared unrelated to treatment. Significant histologic changes observed in association with exposures of 0.005 to 0.05 ppm appeared to be adaptive; based on biochemical, hematological, and histological data, a dietary NOAEL for the study was 0.5 ppm.

StringWithMarkup.String: Octachlorostyrene is not produced commercially for any application. In addition to the lower chlorinated styrenes, octachlorostyrene is mainly an accidental by-product of high temperature industrial processes involving chlorine. Documented release of octachlorostyrene into the environment has largely occurred via waste water effluents from chlorine gas, magnesium, niobium and tantalum production and the smelting of aluminum. Release of octachlorostyrene to the environment has also been reported as leachate from an industrial landfill and fly ash from waste incinerators. If released to air, an estimated vapor pressure of 1.3X10-5 mm Hg at 25 °C indicates octachlorostyrene will exist in both the vapor and particulate phases in the ambient atmosphere. Vapor-phase octachlorostyrene will be degraded in the atmosphere by reaction with photochemically-produced hydroxyl radicals; the half-life for this reaction in air is estimated to be 15 days. Particulate-phase octachlorostyrene will be removed from the atmosphere by wet and dry deposition. Octachlorostyrene weakly adsorbs UV light between 295 and 310 nm and slow photolysis is observed. If released to soil, octachlorostyrene is expected to have no mobility based upon Koc values from 200,000 to 10,000,000. Volatilization from moist soil surfaces is expected to be an important fate process based upon an estimated Henry's Law constant of 2.3X10-4 atm-cu m/mole. However, adsorption to soil is expected to attenuate volatilization. If released into water, octachlorostyrene is expected to adsorb to suspended solids and sediment based upon its Koc. Volatilization from water surfaces is expected to be an important fate process based upon this compound's estimated Henry's Law constant. Estimated volatilization half-lives for a model river and model lake are 13 hrs and 10 days, respectively. However, volatilization from water surfaces is expected to be attenuated by adsorption to suspended solids and sediment in the water column. BCF values ranging from 8,100 to 1,400,000 suggests bioconcentration in aquatic organisms is very high. Hydrolysis is not expected to occur due to the lack of hydrolyzable functional groups. Occupational exposure to octachlorostyrene may occur through inhalation of dust and dermal contact with this compound at workplaces where octachlorostyrene is produced indirectly. Monitoring data indicate that the general population may be exposed to octachlorostyrene via ingestion of fish and seafood containing octachlorostyrene. (SRC)

Section.Description: Sorption to soils and sediments is an important factor on the transport and fate of organic contaminants in the environment.  The soil/water adsorption coefficient, also known as solid-water distribution coefficient (Kd), measures the amount of chemical substance adsorbed onto soil per amount of water.  Since adsorption occurs predominantly by partition into the soil organic matter, it is more useful to normalize the Kd value to the organic carbon content of a soil and express the distribution coefficient in Koc (organic carbon normalized distribution coefficient).  The greater the Kd (or Koc) value, the less likely a chemical will leach or contribute to runoff.  A very high value means it is strongly adsorbed onto soil and organic matter and does not move throughout the soil.

StringWithMarkup.String: The Henry's Law constant for octachlorostyrene is estimated as 2.3X10-4 atm-cu m/mole(SRC) using a fragment constant estimation method(1). This Henry's Law constant indicates that octachlorostyrene is expected to volatilize from water surfaces(2). Based on this Henry's Law constant, the volatilization half-life from a model river (1 m deep, flowing 1 m/sec, wind velocity of 3 m/sec)(2) is estimated as 13 hours(SRC). The volatilization half-life from a model lake (1 m deep, flowing 0.05 m/sec, wind velocity of 0.5 m/sec)(2) is estimated as 10 days(SRC). Octachlorostyrene's Henry's Law constant indicates that volatilization from moist soil surfaces may occur(SRC). However, volatilization from moist soil water surfaces is expected to be attenuated by adsorption(SRC). The estimated volatilization half-life from a model pond is 670 yrs if adsorption is considered(3). Octachlorostyrene is not expected to volatilize from dry soil surfaces(SRC) based upon an estimated vapor pressure of 1.3X10-5 mm Hg(SRC), determined from a fragment constant method(4).
